title: Read, predict and revise with evidence

prompts: Without the worked example, explain: Make a plausible prediction from a story detail and revise it when new information appears.
Without the worked example, explain: Ask a question that can guide further reading and distinguish an unanswered question from a known fact.

pedagogy.rationale: Read a story in two parts so predictions precede the ending. Compare claims with selected evidence, then independently summarize and revise an explanation.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Read a short narrative with oral or scribed support, identify its characters and explain a simple cause and effect.

misconceptions.description: A plausible prediction is reported as something the story has already established.
misconceptions.response: Name the detail that makes the idea plausible, use might or may, and change the prediction if later evidence conflicts.

misconceptions.description: A summary lists incidental details or invents an outcome instead of connecting the central problem, response and result.
misconceptions.response: Keep the problem, the action taken and the result supported by the story; remove details that do not explain that connection.

scenes.title: Pause before the ending
scenes.learnerAction: Read the two paragraphs, then write or say a prediction using might and one supporting detail.

content.body: Read only the opening for now. Picture the difficulty the class faces. Find the detail that explains why clear labels matter. Keep the ending closed while you make your first prediction.

prompts.prompt: What might Massa do next? Use one detail from the opening to explain why your prediction is plausible. Ask one question you want the ending to answer.

accessibility.textAlternative: Read only the opening for now. Picture the difficulty the class faces. Find the detail that explains why clear labels matter. Keep the ending closed while you make your first prediction. Massa and the garden labels: opening. After rain, the names on the school garden labels were hard to read. Massa found the spare labels beside the seedlings. The class planned to share seedlings on Friday. If the names disappeared, visitors might not know which plants they were taking. Massa carried a clean tin under the veranda. She put spare labels inside, but left the lid nearby. 'Will this help us keep the names clear?' she asked. The next shower had not arrived. What might Massa do next? Use one detail from the opening to explain why your prediction is plausible. Ask one question you want the ending to answer.

blocks.title: Massa and the garden labels: opening
paragraphs: After rain, the names on the school garden labels were hard to read. Massa found the spare labels beside the seedlings. The class planned to share seedlings on Friday. If the names disappeared, visitors might not know which plants they were taking.
Massa carried a clean tin under the veranda. She put spare labels inside, but left the lid nearby. 'Will this help us keep the names clear?' she asked. The next shower had not arrived.

scenes.title: Show the difference between a clue and a fact
scenes.learnerAction: Identify the stated detail, the tentative prediction and the question that could guide the next reading.

content.body: A reader thinks: Massa moved the tin under a roof, so she might try sheltering the labels. The movement is a stated detail. Sheltering is a prediction because we have not read the result yet. A useful question is: Will the names stay readable after rain?

hints: Look for the action the narrator explicitly describes.
The opening says the next shower has not arrived; no rain-test outcome is known yet.

accessibility.textAlternative: A reader thinks: Massa moved the tin under a roof, so she might try sheltering the labels. The movement is a stated detail. Sheltering is a prediction because we have not read the result yet. A useful question is: Will the names stay readable after rain? Which statement is already known from the opening? Options: Massa carried a tin under the veranda.; Every label will stay clear all week.; The class has already shared the seedlings..

scenes.title: Choose evidence and a useful question
scenes.learnerAction: Select both relevant details and choose a useful unanswered question, explaining how each connects to the problem.

content.body: A prediction should fit the difficulty in the story. A question helps when its answer would change or deepen your understanding. Select the details that explain why readable labels matter, then choose a question the opening leaves unresolved.

hints: Look for the link between the unreadable names and the visitors' choices.
An unanswered question asks for information the opening has not supplied.

accessibility.textAlternative: A prediction should fit the difficulty in the story. A question helps when its answer would change or deepen your understanding. Which two details explain why the class needs readable labels? Which question is still open and useful? Options: Will the labels stay clear after another shower?; Did Massa carry a tin?; What is Massa's favourite song?.

sentences.text: After rain, the names on the school garden labels were hard to read.
sentences.why: This identifies the problem with the labels.

sentences.text: If the names disappeared, visitors might not know which plants they were taking.
sentences.why: This explains why the problem matters for sharing seedlings.

sentences.text: Massa carried a clean tin under the veranda.
sentences.why: This is an action toward a possible response; it does not explain why the visitors need names.

items.prompt: Which question is still open and useful?

options.text: Will the labels stay clear after another shower?
options.feedback: The opening gives no test result. This question checks whether the idea could address the problem.
The text already answers this directly; it does not guide the next investigation.
The opening gives no reason to connect this detail with the label problem.

scenes.title: Read what happened next
scenes.learnerAction: Read both paragraphs and mark one detail that confirms, changes or limits your first prediction.

content.body: Now read the ending. Compare it with your prediction before changing any words. A different outcome does not make the earlier prediction dishonest if it was reasonable from the opening. Good readers update their thinking.

accessibility.textAlternative: Now read the ending. Compare it with your prediction before changing any words. A different outcome does not make the earlier prediction dishonest if it was reasonable from the opening. Good readers update their thinking. Massa and the garden labels: ending. Massa's class put one spare label on an open bench and another inside the tin under the veranda. Both labels used the same paper and ink. After a shower, the bench label was hard to read. The sheltered label was still clear. The class repeated the comparison after another shower and saw the same pattern. They kept spare labels in the sheltered tin and checked them before sharing the seedlings. They had not tested every kind of rain. If later checks showed a problem, they would change the plan.

scenes.title: Separate a supported result from a sweeping claim
scenes.learnerAction: Choose the justified conclusion and strongest summary, then explain what each rejected claim adds or leaves out.

content.body: Work independently with the complete story. A result from two comparisons supports a particular conclusion, but it does not tell us what would happen in every possible storm. Decide which interpretation and summary preserve what the text actually shows.

accessibility.textAlternative: Work independently with the complete story. A result from two comparisons supports a particular conclusion, but it does not tell us what would happen in every possible storm. Decide which interpretation and summary preserve what the text actually shows. Which conclusion is supported by the ending? Options: The tin will protect every label in every storm forever.; The open-bench label stayed clearer in both comparisons.; The sheltered label stayed clearer in the two comparisons described.. Which short account best connects the problem, response and result? Options: Massa sold all the plants after proving that no label could ever blur again.; Massa had a tin. There were seedlings. Friday was coming.; Rain blurred the garden labels. The class compared open and sheltered labels, then kept spare labels sheltered after two clearer results..

items.prompt: Which conclusion is supported by the ending?

options.text: The tin will protect every label in every storm forever.
options.feedback: The story explicitly says that not every kind of rain was tested.

options.text: The open-bench label stayed clearer in both comparisons.
options.feedback: The ending reports that the bench label became hard to read; this reverses the evidence.

options.text: The sheltered label stayed clearer in the two comparisons described.
options.feedback: This matches the reported results without extending them to every possible kind of rain.

items.prompt: Which short account best connects the problem, response and result?

options.text: Massa sold all the plants after proving that no label could ever blur again.
options.feedback: The text reports neither sales nor a guarantee about every future label.

options.text: Massa had a tin. There were seedlings. Friday was coming.
options.feedback: These details do not explain how the class responded or what the comparison showed.

options.text: Rain blurred the garden labels. The class compared open and sheltered labels, then kept spare labels sheltered after two clearer results.
options.feedback: This connects the central problem, the response and the reported outcome.

scenes.title: Write an evidence-based summary
scenes.learnerAction: Write a 30 to 60 word summary and one question that the story leaves open.

content.body: Write for a classmate who has not read the story. Include the central problem, the class's response and the result. Use your own words. Keep one limit of the evidence in mind rather than promising that the idea will always work.

prompts.prompt: Summarize the problem, response and result in 30 to 60 words. Then ask one unanswered question whose answer could change or improve the class's plan.

accessibility.textAlternative: Write for a classmate who has not read the story. Include the central problem, the class's response and the result. Use your own words. scenes.title: Make one claim more precise
scenes.learnerAction: Show one before-and-after revision and explain why it is more faithful to the text.

content.body: Reread your prediction and summary. Replace an unsupported claim with a detail from the story, or remove a detail that does not help explain the main event. A partner may read the text aloud while you direct the revision.

prompts.prompt: Quote one sentence from your own first attempt and write its improved version. Explain the story evidence behind your change. For an advanced challenge, describe a possible new test result that would make you revise the class's recommendation.
